engine_label: Claude (Sonnet) via claude -p, web search on
question: How do I build a lead list of new apartment buildings to sell to?
answer:
Building a lead list of new apartment buildings for B2B sales usually comes down to two problems: (1) finding out *where* new buildings are being built or delivered, and (2) finding *who* to contact once you know the address. Here's how people typically do both.

## 1. Data sources for finding new buildings

**Paid, purpose-built for this:**
- **Yardi Matrix** — the standard for multifamily construction pipeline and lease-up tracking (units under construction, planned, and recently delivered, by metro/submarket). Most CRE sales teams targeting multifamily use this or CoStar.
- **CoStar** — broadest commercial real estate database; tracks new deliveries, under-construction properties, ownership, and property management company. Expensive but comprehensive.
- **RealPage (Real Data / Market Analytics)** — similar to Yardi Matrix, strong on lease-up and occupancy data, useful if you're targeting properties still filling units.
- **Zonda** — strong on new construction/permit data, originally single-family focused but has multifamily coverage.
- **Dodge Construction Network (Dodge Data & Analytics)** — tracks construction starts and permits, good for catching buildings at the pre-construction/groundbreaking stage, which is often the best time to get in front of a developer before vendor decisions are locked in.

**Cheaper / free-ish:**
- **Local city/county building permit portals** (open data portals — many cities publish permit data as CSV/API, e.g. Socrata-based portals). Slower and more manual, but free and often more current than paid databases in a single metro.
- **BuildZoom** — aggregates permit data nationally, searchable by project type.
- **LoopNet / Crexi** — commercial listings, sometimes show new multifamily assets for sale or lease.
- **Apartments.com / Apartment List / RentCafe** — searchable by "new construction" or lease-up status; useful for confirming a building is actively leasing (i.e., staffed and operational).

**Trade press (good for catching deals and openings you'd otherwise miss):**
- **Multi-Housing News**, **REBusinessOnline**, **GlobeSt.com**, **Bisnow** (regional editions) — cover groundbreakings, openings, and ownership/management changes.
- **NMHC (National Multifamily Housing Council)** — publishes the "NMHC 50," annual rankings of the largest owners, developers, and managers. Good for identifying the big players to target account-based.

**Brokers as a shortcut:** Multifamily brokerage teams at **CBRE, JLL, Cushman & Wakefield, Marcus & Millichap, Berkadia, Walker & Dunlop** track every new delivery in their coverage metro. A relationship with one broker can save you a lot of database work, though they'll expect something in return (referrals, info).

## 2. Turning addresses into contacts

Once you have a list of buildings/projects, you need the actual decision-maker (property manager, regional manager, developer's VP of construction, etc., depending on what you're selling):
- **LinkedIn Sales Navigator** — filter by company (the property management company) + title (leasing manager, community manager, regional VP).
- **Apollo.io** or **ZoomInfo** — bulk contact enrichment once you know the management company.
- Identify the **management company** first — large ones repeat across many buildings (**Greystar, Lincoln Property Company, AvalonBay, Camden Property Trust, Mill Creek Residential, Cortland, Bell Partners, Asset Living, FPI Management**, etc.). Selling to the regional/corporate level of one of these can open doors to dozens of properties at once instead of chasing one building at a time.

## 3. Practical workflow

1. Define target criteria: metro(s), unit count minimum, building class, and timing (pre-construction vs. actively leasing vs. stabilized — the right timing depends heavily on what you're selling).
2. Pull the pipeline list from Yardi Matrix/CoStar or permit data for your target metros.
3. Cross-reference addresses against management company (Matrix/CoStar usually list this directly).
4. Enrich with contacts via Sales Navigator/Apollo.
5. Load into a CRM and prioritize by delivery date — buildings 3–9 months from opening are typically making vendor decisions, so that window is usually the highest-value target.

If you tell me what you're actually selling (amenities, tech/software, maintenance services, supplies, etc.), I can narrow this down — the right data source and the right buying window change a lot depending on the product.
